params.question: Why is a KOH mount particularly valuable when a suspected fungal lesion has an atypical clinical appearance?

answers.text: It identifies the exact dermatophyte species to guide antifungal selection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A KOH mount only confirms the presence of fungal elements (hyphae or spores). It cannot identify the species — that requires a fungal culture.

answers.text: It confirms the fungal aetiology when prior steroid use or lookalike conditions make clinical diagnosis unreliable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When steroid-antifungal combination creams mask the classic ring-shaped morphology (tinea incognito), or when eczema and psoriasis mimic a fungal infection, the KOH mount provides cheap, rapid bedside confirmation before committing to weeks of systemic antifungal therapy.

answers.text: It reveals whether the fungus has developed resistance to topical antifungals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A KOH mount cannot assess antifungal resistance. Resistance testing requires fungal culture with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination.

answers.text: It assesses the depth of fungal invasion to decide between topical and systemic therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: KOH mounting shows fungal elements in scraped material but cannot assess depth of invasion. The choice between topical and systemic therapy depends on the site, extent, and chronicity of the infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The primary value of KOH in atypical presentations is confirming the diagnosis. Steroid misuse creates tinea incognito, and conditions like eczema or psoriasis can mimic fungal infection — starting antifungals without confirmation wastes time and resources.

The KOH mount is the first-line bedside test precisely because it gives a quick, cheap answer when clinical appearances are misleading — confirming fungal aetiology before committing to potentially hepatotoxic systemic therapy.

params.question: A 25-year-old woman with extensive, recurrent tinea corporis has completed a full course of oral terbinafine without improvement. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

answers.text: Repeat terbinafine at a higher dose for a longer duration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Simply escalating the dose of a failed first-line agent is not the resistance-aware approach. Treatment failure with terbinafine should prompt a switch to an alternative systemic antifungal.

answers.text: Prescribe a topical steroid-antifungal combination cream to reduce inflammation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Steroid-antifungal combination creams are a major driver of spread, tinea incognito, and antifungal resistance in India. They must be stopped, not added.

answers.text: Discontinue all antifungals and observe for spontaneous resolution over six weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Extensive, recurrent dermatophytosis will not resolve spontaneously. Active treatment with an alternative systemic agent is required, along with addressing predisposing factors and household contacts.

answers.text: Switch to oral itraconazole as a second-line systemic agent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When first-line terbinafine fails in chronic or recurrent dermatophytosis, the current resistance-aware standard is to switch to itraconazole rather than repeating the same drug.

overallFeedback.feedback: When first-line terbinafine fails in extensive or recurrent dermatophytosis, the rational next step is to switch to oral itraconazole — not to repeat the same drug, add steroid combinations, or observe passively.

Switching to itraconazole after terbinafine failure is the current resistance-aware standard. Always also address predisposing factors, treat household contacts, and stop any steroid-antifungal combination creams.
